Notes

打哈哈

打哈哈 is to joke or laugh in order to brush something aside, often instead of giving a serious answer. This is a demand for accountability, not a general instruction to stop being happy. The later blocks of 哈哈哈 answer that demand with exactly the laughter it tries to prohibit.

  • Genius community transcript
人民群众

人民群众 means “the masses” or “the people”; 民生问题 means issues affecting people’s livelihoods. The formal civic vocabulary turns a complaint about bitten bottoms into a mock public-affairs report. That change of register is audible in the language itself.

  • Genius community transcript
咸鸭蛋瞎操心

The line pairs salted food with needless worry, echoing the shape of 咸吃萝卜淡操心, a saying about meddling or worrying over matters that are not your business. Here duck eggs take the radish’s place. 咸, “salty,” and 闲, “idle,” are both xián, adding a second route from the snack to having too much time to worry.

  • Genius community transcript
  • Hu Hongxia: the saying in use
龙抬头

龙抬头, “the dragon raises its head,” names the traditional festival on the second day of the second lunar month. The next line replaces that auspicious upward movement with everyone lifting their backsides: the joke depends on hearing the two images together.

  • Ministry of Culture: the Longtaitou custom
洗地

洗地 literally means wash the floor; in online argument it also means excuse, defend or whitewash someone’s discreditable actions. Kneeling and using tears make that figurative cleanup into humiliating physical labor. Both the floor and the act of covering for someone remain available in the image.

  • Genius community transcript
  • People’s Daily: an example of figurative 洗地
伤不起

The 不起 construction marks something one cannot afford or withstand: compare 买不起, “cannot afford to buy.” 伤不起 extends it to getting hurt—emotionally, physically or materially. Following a line about kneeling, it gives the boastful voice a brief admission that another hit could cost too much.

  • Genius community transcript
上好佳

上好佳 is the Chinese name of Oishi, the snack brand. The phrase divides as 换 / 上好佳的 / 也行: “switching to Oishi’s is fine too.” Reading 换上 as one verb would hide the brand name. The preceding shrimp-stick line makes this a casual snack substitution.

  • Oishi China: brand and products
老子

老子 can literally mean “father,” but here it is an aggressive first-person pronoun: an “I” that talks down to the listener. The translation adds a swear word to carry that attitude; it is not introducing the speaker’s father into the scene.

  • Genius community transcript
后现代的温柔

The final repeated phrase calls the preceding knife-and-phlegm image “postmodern tenderness.” Reading “tenderness” straight would lose the collision: the lyric places a gentle label on a grotesquely invasive act.

  • Genius community transcript
